node.name: Volunteer with Sunrise Cafe!
node.descriptionText:
Start your morning off on a great note! Join Dwight Hall Monday and Wednesday mornings to volunteer at Sunrise Cafe. Sunrise Cafe is an early morning soup kitchen that serves New Haven's homeless and food-insecure every weekday from 6:30 A.M. to 8:30 A.M. The service site is located at 57 Olive St., just a 15 minute walk from Phelps Gate. Volunteers will meet in front of Phelps Gate at 6:00am, walk together to Sunrise Cafe, and will return to campus by 9:00am.

To sign up, please request to join DWIGHT HALL VOLUNTEER CORPS, and we will approve your request as soon as possible.

Sunrise Cafe has been serving breakfast without charge to New Haven's homeless and hungry since 2015. Each weekday morning, the Cafe welcomes guests to the undercroft of St. Paul and St. James, near Wooster Square and three blocks south of the New Haven Green with white tablecloths, flowers and a rotating menu of fresh, warm, nutritious home-cooked food. Your generosity opens our doors.

Cheerful volunteers take each order individually, deliver the breakfast to our guest and help our paid chefs in the kitchen. Staff and volunteers ensure every guest is warmly welcomed.

Sunrise Cafe is uniquely welcoming and secure, based on trust and mutual respect, and the rapport built between the volunteer servers and our guests. With a warm welcome and just two rules – no drugs on the premises and no arguments – Sunrise has become a community center for the homeless, a place to come every weekday morning and gather with friends.

Hungry friends come for the home-cooked, nourishing breakfast and stay for simple medical services offered by the Cornell Scott Health Center and access to support from social services to find housing.

Sunrise provides a unique opportunity to bridge New Haven's inequalities that separate us from one another. Volunteers come once and become regulars. Guests and volunteers become friends and greet one another on the street.

If you have any questions, email maryann.dang@yale.edu

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: Children’s Clothing Swap
node.descriptionText:
Attention Yale families! Yale Grad Housing, the Office of International Students and Scholars, and the Office of Sustainability are co-hosting a children's clothing event. 
 
We have children's clothing available to members of the Yale community, free of charge! Participants will have the opportunity to browse through the Swap Room’s collection of gently used clothing items and shoes, brought to main campus for this event, and take what they would like, all for free. The purpose of the event is to reduce and divert clothing waste and promote a circular economy at Yale. 

Coffee and tea will be provided. Please bring your own reusable bag. Advance registration is required. 

Note: Donations are not required to participate. If you would like to donate clothes prior to the event, please drop them at the OISS front desk during their business hours (Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from 9AM to 12PM and 1 to 5PM) two weeks before the event (weeks of October 19 and 26). Parents are allowed to bring clothing items to share if they wish, provided that they are children sizes (newborn to youth), and are washed, clean, and in good condition. This swap is strictly for clothing. Other items such as books, toys, pillows, sheets, strollers, etc., will not be accepted as donations.

node.name: BIOMES: Advancing integrated continental to global scale hydrology through democratized data and ml-accelerated modeling presented by Reed M. Maxwell, Princeton University
node.descriptionText:
About the Seminar: 
Understanding water availability, predicting droughts and floods, requires a top-to-bottom accounting of the water cycle from treetops to bedrock. Groundwater supports half the global population, 50% of crop production, and a wide array of ecosystems. However, we lack high fidelity physically accurate models that capture the entire hydrologic cycle including groundwater.   Groundwater is so sparsely observed that it cannot be simulated by data-driven statistical or machine-learning approaches alone. This limitation can be addressed with physically-based models, but only at great computational costs. The CONUS2.1 platform is a high-resolution, physically-based model that couples surface and subsurface hydrology, enabling the simulation of complex processes such as groundwater-surface water interactions, evapotranspiration, and land-atmosphere feedbacks.  We are evolving this platform into the first digital twin of the full terrestrial hydrologic cycle across the United States.  Using AI to accelerate our solutions we will be able to develop a platform that is operational in real time. The model will be continuously updated and improved with new information from remote sensing products and gauge observations. In addition to presenting the digital twin, this talk will focus on a number of recent advancements that leverage GPU acceleration, machine learning emulation and dynamic downscaling of physical processes to accelerate this platform.
 

Reed Maxwell is the William and Edna Macaleer Professor of Engineering and Applied Science at Princeton University, with appointments in Civil and Environmental Engineering and the High Meadows Environmental Institute. He studies where freshwater goes — underground, downhill, and into the atmosphere — and how drought, climate, and human demand are changing that cycle. His group tracks groundwater with continental-scale computer models, machine learning, and drone-based fieldwork in the headwaters of the Colorado River. He directs the Integrated GroundWater Modeling Center, is a Fellow of the American Geophysical Union, and has authored more than 200 peer-reviewed journal articles.

node.name: The Persian Gulf as a Waterway and Region: A History of the Current War
node.descriptionText: Arang Keshavarzian is professor of Middle Eastern and Islamic Studies at New York University. He is the author of Bazaar and State in Iran: The Politics of the Tehran Marketplace, and coeditor with Ali Mirsepassi of Global 1979: Geographies and Histories of the Iranian Revolution. His most recent book, Making Space for the Gulf: Histories of Regionalism and the Middle East (Stanford University Press, 2024), received the 2025 Roger Owen Prize from the Middle East Studies Association as well as an honorary mention for the 2025 biennial book award from the Association for Gulf and Arabian Peninsula Studies.

node.name: Yale AI Updates + Community Chat: Teaching & Learning - Featuring Yale's Clarity Platform
node.descriptionText:
Exploring Yale's Clarity Platform
Join us for a live online session focused on how AI is shaping teaching and learning at Yale. This month, we will take a closer look at Yale's newly upgraded Clarity Platform and explore how faculty, students, and staff can use it for teaching, learning, and everyday work.

We will share recent AI updates and demonstrate Clarity's new experience, including its range of AI models, Featured Agents, file uploads, image generation, voice conversations, and other new features. We will also highlight practical teaching and learning use cases and discuss how instructors might incorporate Clarity into their courses.

We will also spend time discussing classroom AI policies, expectations for student use, and considerations for using AI thoughtfully and responsibly. As always, the final portion of the session will be open for community questions, ideas, and conversation.

Agenda
30 Minutes: AI Tools, Updates, and Clarity Platform
An overview of Yale's AI tools and resources, followed by a demonstration of the newly upgraded Clarity Platform and examples of teaching and learning use cases.

10 Minutes: Classroom AI Policies and Considerations
Ideas and considerations for setting expectations around AI use and deciding how tools like Clarity may fit into your course.

20 Minutes: Community Questions & Answers
An open conversation for questions, use cases, ideas, and discussion with colleagues across Yale.

node.name: Interwoven: Sounds and Visions from the World’s Refugee Camps
node.descriptionText:
This retrospective exhibition of community art and traditional music will be on view at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music’s Miller Hall at 406 Prospect Street, New Haven from October 15 -December 3 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 12 - 4 p.m., except for Thanksgiving week when the ISM is closed.

Presented by Artolution, an international community-based public arts, education, and mental health organization that uses creative expression to build connection, resilience, and community, the exhibition is organized by Dr. Max Frieder, Artolution Co-Founder and Chief Creative Officer (read more about Dr. Frieder below).

Building on the acclaimed exhibition Interwoven: Exchange Artworks Made Between Refugee Camps Around the World, originally launched at the United Nations, this expanded presentation hosted at the ISM brings together large-scale collaborative artworks, video documentation of traditional folkloric musicians, and cultural artifacts created by displaced communities across five continents.

The exhibition creates a dialogue between visual art and music in contexts of displacement and crisis. Alongside the artworks, visitors encounter videos of musicians from the same communities, offering an opportunity to experience not only the remarkable stories behind the works, but also the sounds, movements, languages, rhythms, and creative traditions of the people who made them.

Together, these works offer a powerful portrait of communities using art, music, and cultural expression to preserve identity, share their stories, and create connections across borders.

node.name: Artist Talk | Richard Long on "Gravity"
node.descriptionText:
In this special conversation at the Yale Center for British Art, acclaimed British artist Richard Long talks about his installation, "Gravity," a site-specific work conceived for the YCBA’s Entrance Court, with James Meyer, curator of modern art at the National Gallery of Art.

This program is free to attend; registration is not required.

---

About the speaker:

Richard Long has been in the vanguard of conceptual art in Britain since he created A Line Made by Walking over half a century ago in 1967, while still a student. This photograph of the path left by his feet in the grass, a fixed line of movement, established a precedent that art could be a journey. Through this medium of walking, time, space, and distance became new subjects for his art. From that time he expanded his walks to wilderness regions all over the world, including a walk in the Alps that was documented by his first text work for the seminal exhibition of minimal and conceptual works titled When Attitude Becomes Form at the Kunsthalle Bern in 1969. After 1969, he began making journeys and sculptures in wilderness places all around the world.

In the 1980s, Long began making new types of mud works using handprints applied directly to the wall. He also continued to make large sculptures of lines and circles from slate, driftwood, footprints, or stone, often sourced from quarries near the exhibition sites. Long mediates on his experience of these places, from mountains through to deserts, shorelines, grasslands, rivers, and snowscapes, according to archetypal geometric marks and shapes, made by his footsteps alone or gathered from the materials of the place. These walks and temporary works of passage are recorded with photographs, maps and text works, where measurements of time and distance, place names, and phenomena are vocabulary for both original ideas and powerful, condensed narratives.

Long was born in Bristol, UK, in 1945 and he lives and works between London and Bristol. He studied at the West of England College of Art, Bristol (1962–65), then St Martin’s School of Art, London (1966–68).

This event is open to all Yale students, faculty, and staff.
If you need technical assistance with registration or require accessible accommodations contact ysc.info@yale.edu.

The votes are in. What can we learn from them? 

Join Dean Pericles Lewis and Professor Gregory Huber for a timely conversation the day after the election. Drawing on the latest results and data, Professor Huber will look beyond the headlines to explore what the numbers reveal about voters, turnout, political behavior, and emerging trends in American politics. Come see democracy in action—and learn how one of Yale’s experts on elections and political behavior makes sense of an election while the story is still unfolding. Light refreshments will be served.

node.name: When It All Feels Like Too Much: Understanding and working with our nervous system
node.descriptionText:
This workshop consists of four learning segments:

1. Understanding the nervous system: we’ll learn the basics of the polyvagal understanding of the nervous system, as well as the concept of the window of tolerance.

2. Dysregulation: we’ll learn how to identify physiological and cognitive/affective symptoms of hyper- and hypo-arousal, which can occur from the onset of overwhelm, distress, fear, etc.)

3. Somatic and breath practices: we’ll learn specific practices using the body and breath, which themselves draw upon and advance mindfulness, to bring us back into the window of tolerance.

4. Interaction with meditation: we’ll learn both how meditation expands the window of tolerance and how to bring ourselves back into a window of tolerance (reregulate) during meditation when we’ve gotten activated.

Beginners and all are welcome.
Taught by Sumi Kim, Buddhist Chaplain.
